blocks.text: Genesis begins with universal origins in chapters 1–11, then turns in chapters 12–50 to the ancestral family narratives, ending with Jacob’s household in Egypt. This movement places Genesis 1 at the broad opening of a book that will progressively narrow its focus from the whole world to one family.

Genesis 1 presents creation as an ordered work: God speaks, separates, names, appoints, blesses, and evaluates what is made. A Babylonian creation epic also moves from divine succession and combat to the ordering of the cosmos and Marduk’s supremacy. The shared attention to waters, cosmic order, celestial organization, and divine rule makes comparison useful, but it does not make the accounts equivalent or demonstrate direct borrowing.

Later Christian writings return to this chapter’s opening language in distinct ways. John 1 portrays the Logos as with God in the beginning, active in creation and life, and later becoming flesh; its interpretation is informed by Jewish Scripture, wisdom and divine-word traditions, as well as Greek discourse. Another text uses “Let there be light” as a theological metaphor for God shining in human hearts, not as a scientific explanation of cognition or vision.

The “image” language of Genesis 1:26–27 is also used in later Christian writings. Messiah is called the image of the invisible God, and the new humanity is described as being renewed in knowledge according to the creator’s image across ethnic, ritual, cultural, and legal distinctions.

Genesis 1:20–28 names living creatures in a wide creation-scale sweep: sea life, birds, land animals, and humans. Zephaniah 1:2–3 similarly sweeps through humans, animals, birds, and fish in announcing judgment. Many readers understand that later passage as creation reversal, with resonances of the flood story.
